Part I describes the development of an intelligent acoustic emission locator, whereas Part II focuses on the related problems of blind source separation, time delay estimation, and the localization of two simultaneous continuous acoustic emission sources.

Locating acoustic emissions in complex aircraft frame structures is a difficult and important task in non-destructive testing. Such structures often have complicated geometries, variable material properties, joints, stiffeners, and boundaries that affect the propagation of acoustic waves. These factors make it challenging to determine the exact origin of an acoustic emission using conventional methods, particularly when wave paths are not simple or when multiple sources are active at the same time.

The intelligent acoustic emission locator presented in Part I is based on the use of a sensor antenna combined with a general regression neural network. Instead of relying solely on analytical models of wave propagation, the system learns the relationship between measured sensor signals and source locations from example data. During training, acoustic emissions are generated or recorded at known positions, and the corresponding sensor responses are stored. The neural network then uses this information to estimate the location of new, unknown acoustic emission events.

Experimental tests showed that the accuracy of the locator depends on several factors. These include the velocity of sound in the tested structure, the attenuation of the acoustic waves, the dimensions of the tested area, and the quality and completeness of the stored training data. Accurate and representative reference data are especially important, since the neural network’s performance depends directly on the examples from which it learns.

The intelligent locator was found to achieve a level of accuracy comparable to that of conventional triangulation methods. However, it offers an important advantage: it does not require detailed analysis of sonic ray paths through the structure. This makes the approach more broadly applicable to complex aircraft frame components, where traditional triangulation can be difficult to implement reliably. By learning from measured data rather than depending entirely on simplified propagation models, the intelligent acoustic emission locator provides a flexible and practical tool for non-destructive evaluation of complex structures.

Locating acoustic emission sources in complex aircraft frame structures is an important but difficult problem in non-destructive testing and structural health monitoring. When a crack, impact, delamination, or other damage mechanism occurs, it can generate transient elastic waves that propagate through the structure and may be detected by acoustic emission sensors. In principle, the arrival times of these waves can be used to determine the position of the source. However, aircraft frame structures are geometrically complicated, contain stiffeners, joints, rivets, changes in thickness, and material discontinuities, and often cause wave reflection, scattering, dispersion, and mode conversion. These effects make conventional source-location methods, particularly those based on idealized triangulation and known sonic ray paths, difficult to apply reliably.

To address this problem, an intelligent acoustic emission source locator is proposed. The system uses a sensor antenna, consisting of multiple acoustic emission sensors arranged on the structure, together with a general regression neural network trained from experimental examples. Instead of explicitly calculating the propagation path of the acoustic waves or relying on simplified assumptions about wave speed and geometry, the method learns the relationship between measured sensor signals and known source positions. During training, acoustic emission events are generated at selected locations on the aircraft frame structure, and the corresponding features recorded by the sensor array are used as input data for the neural network. Once trained, the network can estimate the location of an unknown acoustic emission source from newly acquired sensor data.

Experimental tests were carried out to evaluate the performance of the proposed locator. The results showed that the neural-network-based system was able to locate acoustic emission sources with an accuracy comparable to that obtained using conventional triangulation methods. At the same time, the intelligent locator offers an important advantage: it does not require detailed analysis of sonic ray paths, which can be extremely difficult or impractical in complex aircraft structures. Because the method is based on training examples rather than a complete analytical model of wave propagation, it can be adapted more easily to structures with complicated geometry and uncertain propagation characteristics.

These findings indicate that a general regression neural network combined with an acoustic emission sensor antenna is a promising approach for aircraft structural monitoring. The method provides a practical means of locating damage-related acoustic events in complex frames and could contribute to more effective non-destructive inspection, early damage detection, and condition-based maintenance of aircraft structures.

**The Part This Plays**

The word **“the”** may seem small, but it has an important part in language. It helps point to something specific, turning a general idea into a clear one. For example, “a book” could mean any book, but “the book” refers to one particular book.

The word **“part”** reminds us that everything can belong to something larger. A part may be small, but it can still be meaningful. In a story, each part helps build the whole message. In life, each choice can be part of a bigger journey.

The word **“this”** brings attention to the present moment or to something close. It helps us focus on what is right here, right now. When we say “this idea,” “this moment,” or “this part,” we are giving importance to something immediate and specific.

Together, **the**, **part**, and **this** show how even simple words can shape meaning. This is the part of language that makes communication clear, direct, and powerful.

counterfactuals.output: This paper presents an intelligent acoustic emission (AE) source location method for nondestructive testing of aircraft frame structures. The proposed approach employs a compact sensor antenna to capture AE signals generated by damage-related events and uses a general regression neural network (GRNN) to estimate the source position. Unlike conventional triangulation-based AE localization methods, which require accurate wave velocity models and precise arrival-time picking, the proposed data-driven method learns the nonlinear relationship between measured signal features and source coordinates directly from calibration data. AE responses are acquired from multiple sensors mounted on representative aircraft frame components, and relevant time- and amplitude-based features are extracted to train the GRNN locator. Experimental results show that the intelligent locator can accurately identify AE source positions under complex structural propagation conditions, including reflections, mode conversion, and geometric discontinuities typical of aircraft frames. The method demonstrates improved robustness, reduced dependence on prior material and structural modeling, and fast localization capability suitable for real-time structural health monitoring. These findings indicate that the combination of a sensor antenna and GRNN provides an effective nondestructive testing tool for detecting and locating active damage sources in aircraft frame structures.

“**Intelligent Acoustic Emission Locator**” describes an “intelligent” approach to locating acoustic emission (AE) sources—small stress-wave events produced by cracking, impact, friction, or other damage mechanisms—especially in structures where traditional AE triangulation is difficult.

**Part I** focuses on the underlying concept and methodology. It presents an AE source-location system that uses learned relationships between sensor signals and source positions rather than relying only on simple wave-speed assumptions. In conventional AE location, arrival-time differences between sensors are used to triangulate the event, but this works best in simple, homogeneous structures. Part I explains how an intelligent or knowledge-based approach—such as pattern recognition, calibration data, and computational mapping—can be trained to recognize how acoustic waves actually propagate through a given structure.

**Part II** applies the method to more realistic and complex structures, including **complicated aircraft structures**. counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a technical abstract describing a neural-network-based acoustic emission locator, its testing on specimens, factors affecting location accuracy, and comparison with conventional triangulation.
counterfactuals.output:
This paper presents a neural-network-based acoustic emission (AE) source location method for structural health monitoring applications. The proposed locator maps measured AE signal features—such as arrival-time differences, peak amplitude, energy, duration, and frequency-domain descriptors—to source coordinates using a supervised learning model trained on experimentally generated AE events. Unlike conventional triangulation methods, which require accurate wave velocity estimation and precise identification of first-arrival times, the neural-network approach learns the nonlinear relationship between sensor responses and source position directly from calibration data.

The method was evaluated on laboratory specimens instrumented with multiple piezoelectric AE sensors. Artificial AE sources, generated using pencil-lead breaks and controlled impact events, were applied at known locations across the specimen surface. The resulting dataset was divided into training, validation, and test subsets to assess generalization performance. Location accuracy was quantified using the Euclidean distance between the predicted and true source coordinates.

Experimental results show that the neural-network locator can achieve improved robustness compared with conventional time-difference-of-arrival triangulation, particularly in cases involving anisotropic wave propagation, geometric boundaries, sensor coupling variability, and noisy signals. The main factors affecting accuracy were found to include sensor layout, training-point density, signal-to-noise ratio, material heterogeneity, wave-mode dispersion, and consistency of source mechanisms between training and testing. Increasing the number and spatial coverage of calibration points generally reduced prediction error, while poor sensor coupling and sparse training data increased localization uncertainty.

Compared with conventional triangulation, the neural-network method reduced dependence on explicit wave-speed assumptions and minimized errors associated with manual or automated arrival-time picking. However, its performance depended strongly on the representativeness of the training dataset and may require retraining when sensor configuration, material condition, or specimen geometry changes. Overall, the results demonstrate that neural-network-based AE localization is a promising alternative to classical triangulation for complex structures where wave propagation is difficult to model analytically.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

Part I introduces an intelligent AE locator designed to estimate source positions from sensor-array data with improved robustness relative to conventional arrival-time methods. The approach integrates data-driven signal interpretation with localization algorithms to handle propagation uncertainty, noise, and measurement variability, demonstrating accurate source identification under controlled test conditions.

Part II extends the framework to the more challenging case of two simultaneous continuous AE sources. A blind source separation strategy is first applied to decompose mixed sensor recordings into individual source components. Time delays associated with each recovered signal are then estimated and used for localization.
